title: TC1-04540
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of India who is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated March 26, 2021, dismissing her claim for protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of India who is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated March 26, 2021, dismissing her claim for protection. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in assessing her claim, and she asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow her appeal and determine that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, pursuant to sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or to send the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.

I dismiss the appeal and find that the RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, nor a person in need of protection, according to section 97 of the IRPA.

The Appellant fears persecution in India by members of the Dera Sacha Sauda (DSS) because she and members of her family have spoken out against it. The Appellant states that the DSS has 40 million followers as a socio-spiritual organization that preaches and practices humanitarian and selfless services to other. However, the Appellant states that its most current leader, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, had led the organization astray. The leader was convicted of sexual abuse and sentenced to 10 years in jail. The Appellant states that, after Mr. XXXX was convicted, the followers of DDS resorted to brutal protests in several parts of Haryana and Delhi.

In 2007, the Appellant, her son and his family were threatened because of their strong views against the DSS. At that time, a rock with a note threatening their lives was thrown through a glass window of their home. The Appellant and her family went to stay with her brother. The Appellant's son received calls alleging that his house had been burned down; however, when he returned home, he found that the house had not been damaged. The Appellant and her family applied for visitor visas to Canada and planned their vacation for XXXX 2017. The Appellant came to Canada with her family, then left for the United Kingdom to stay with her other son. In XXXX 2017, the Appellant's son received a call that his XXXX XXXX in India had been looted by the DSS followers, who were shouting the family's name threatening to kill him. The Appellant's son and his family filed a refugee claim in Canada in November 2017.

The Appellant returned to India in XXXX 2019. In XXXX 2019, unknown individuals attacked the Appellant's home in search of her son. The Appellant travelled to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 and made a refugee claim in December 2019.
The RPD noted that the Appellant underwent heart surgery in XXXX 2021. The RPD stated that it recognized, and took into consideration, the Appellant's medical condition in reaching its decision.

My role is to look at all of the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 In doing so, I have carried out my own independent analysis of the RPD record, including the RPD's reasons and decision and the transcript of the hearing, to determine whether the RPD erred.
The Appellant does not request that new evidence be admitted.
Owing to the fact that I did not admit any new evidence, I have no authority to hold an oral hearing.
The RPD found that the determinative issues were the lack of credibility and the insufficiency of the supporting evidence.

I find that the RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is not credible and has not provided sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to establish that she faces as serious risk of persecution or that she is a person in need of protection in India.

The RPD found a number of inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence, including: inconsistencies pertaining to a stone throwing incident in 2007, why a police complaint was not filed with respect to that incident, circumstances surrounding the looting of the Appellant's son's XXXX XXXX, who filed the police report concerning this incident, and the alleged XXXX 2019 attacks at her home.

The Appellant raises that a number of grounds in this appeal are not directly related to the RPD's credibility findings. Hence, I will first review the RPD's credibility finding in order to assess if they are correct, and then I will address the Appellant's grounds of appeal. Inconsistency as to the stone throwing incident in 2007

The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from an inconsistency in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form and her testimony concerning what was on a note on a rock that was thrown through a window of the family house in 2007 when they resided in the state of Rajasthan. The RPD found that, while she testified that the note states that the family must follow the DSS religion, her BOC stated that it contained a warning for her son, PrakXXXX, and his family and her to stop expressing their strong views against the DSS and defaming its leader. The RPD found that the Appellant was unable to explain the inconsistency and found that it was a significant discrepancy with respect to her claim for refugee protection. The RPD did not draw any inference from the fact that the Appellant delayed the filing of her claim in Canada and stated that it may be due to the Appellant's health conditions at the time.
The Appellant did not make any submissions with respect to the RPD's finding concerning the 2007 incident. Finding - The inconsistency concerning the 2007 incident is material

In the Appellant's BOC, she states that her fear of harm started in 2007 when she along with her son and his family were threatened because of their views concerning the DSS. She stated that a rock with a note was thrown through a glass window in the family house. In her BOC, she states that the "note warned us to stop expressing our views against Dera and defaming Dera leader."2

In her testimony, however, the Appellant provided a different understanding of what the letter attached to the rock stated. She stated that:3 MEMBER: Again, you are way ahead of me. Can we go back to 2007 when the rock was thrown? The rock was thrown through your window in 2007. CLAIMANT: Yeah, the stone in -- yeah, the -- yes, the stone was thrown in 2007, when I returned from my brother's house with my kids. In that time, they said that, "In reality, if you don't follow us, we will burn your house. Right now, it is not burned, but we will do that."

I find that the RPD did not err in drawing a negative credibility inference from this inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence. What the Appellant stated in her BOC is plainly different than what she stated at the hearing. The Appellant provided no explanation for the inconsistency when asked by the RPD except to say that her agents of harm are "very bad."4 The rock throwing incident is a key reason why she fears the DSS, and I would expect that the Appellant would provide consistent evidence as to the initiating source of her fear.

I also find that the Appellant provided no evidence of who actually threw the note. She only noted that there were two men with their faces covered.5 Police report from an alleged fire at the Appellant's son's house

The RPD found that, after the stone throwing incident, the Appellant, her son, XXXX, and his family, moved to her brother's house. At this time, XXXX received an anonymous telephone call that his house had burned down, and he later discovered it was unharmed. XXXX subsequently received a threat that, if he does not apologize to the DSS, his house will actually be burnt down. The RPD found an inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence as to why the police would not accept a complaint. The RPD found that this inconsistency undercuts the proposition that there is no state protection for the Appellant.
The Appellant did not make any submissions with respect to the RPD's finding concerning the police complaint. Findings - Reason why police report was not filed is a material inconsistency

I find that the RPD did not err in finding an inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence concerning why a police report could not be filed with respect to the rock throwing incident. The Appellant stated in her BOC that a police report could not be filed because the DSS has "so much political power and influence on people."6 In her testimony, the Appellant stated that the DSS do bribe the police, but when the RPD asked directly why no police report was filed, she stated it was because the persons who made the threats could not be identified.7 The Appellant provided no explanation as to why her understanding of the actual reason why the police did not accept the complaint was not mentioned in her BOC. I find that there is a material difference as to why the police would not accept the complaint, that is, because the perpetrators could not be identified versus the police are under the influence of the agents of persecution.

The RPD in its reasons did not expressly make a credibility finding and instead states that this inconsistency undercuts the proposition that there is no state protection. I find that this inconsistency does lead to a negative credibility inference from the inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence. I re-iterate that the Appellant has made no issues with respect to the negative credibility findings or whether there is adequate state protection. Inconsistencies concerning the looting of the Appellant's son's XXXX XXXX

The RPD found inconsistencies as to the looting of the Appellant's son's XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2017. The RPD found that various inconsistencies with respect to whether the Appellant's XXXX was open or closed; whether business was conducted or not; whether XXXX was left open under glass or in the vault; and thus "puts in doubt the claim that a politically motivated looting occurred and the claimant's credibility."8

The RPD found that an affidavit by XXXX XXXX contradicted the Appellant's evidence because the affidavit states that he checked the accounts at the XXXX daily. His affidavit and another one filed by the Appellant did not identify the relationship of Mr. XXXX to the Appellant, while the Appellant identified him as her son-in-law. Findings - inconsistencies and vagueness as to the status of the Appellant's son's XXXX erode the Appellant's credibility

The Appellant wrote in her BOC that her son received a call from XXXX, an employee at his XXXX XXXX in India, stating that, on XXXX XXXX, 2017, the XXXX XXXX had been looted by DSS followers and that they broke all of the glass taking some INR XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX-XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX worth of XXXX.9

However, the Appellant's testimony concerning the looting and the status of the XXXX had a number of inconsistencies. The Appellant testified that her son's XXXX XXXX was closed and no longer operating when her son and his family travelled to Canada in XXXX 2017.10 She then stated that it was open in the XXXX of 2017.11 The Appellant stated that the XXXX did not sell XXXX when her son was in Canada, but then she testified that persons could buy XXXX.12

The RPD then asked how the XXXX could have been looted if the XXXX were in a vault, and the Appellant could not explain except to say that the looters must have broken the glass with a hammer or a stone.13 The Appellant stated that her son-in-law did not review the XXXX accounts because there was no business. When the RPD asked to explain why, in her son-in-law's affidavit, Mr. XXXX states that he did visit the XXXX to review the accounts, but she stated that she did not know anything about this matter.14

I find that the inconsistencies pertaining to circumstances of the looting of the Appellant's son's XXXX erodes her credibility. I also agree with the RPD that there is an inconsistency in the Appellant's testimony and Mr. XXXX affidavit15 where the Appellant states that no one reviewed the XXXX accounts while her son was in Canada, although Mr. XXXX swears that he did undertake such a review.

Although the RPD noted that neither Mr. XXXX affidavit nor the affidavit of XXXX XXXX16 mentions that Mr. XXXX is the Appellant's son-in-law, I do not find this to be a material omission. I do not find that the Appellant was attempting to misrepresent her relationship to Mr. XXXX, and I do not know why the RPD found this omission to be significant. Although I find that the RPD was not correct with respect to this particular finding, it does not impact my overall finding that the RPD's credibility findings were correct.

I also note that the Appellant provided no direct evidence to establish that the DSS is responsible for looting. The Appellant testified that the neighbours stated that they would get threats from the DSS; however, there is no reference to the looting of the XXXX.17 The affidavit by Mr. XXXX relates to what he was told by the employee, Mr. XXXX. In Mr. XXXX affidavit, he states that "labourers residing nearby in the market" heard that the looters saying they were members of "XXXX XXXX" and heard that they threatened the Appellant's son and his family. I do not find that the affidavits provide high probative value as to who was responsible for the looting. Mr. XXXX is relying on what Mr. XXXX told him, and Mr. XXXX is relying on what he heard from neighbours. In light of the inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence, I find that the RPD was correct in finding that there is doubt as to whether the looting was politically motivated, and I find that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the looting was politically motivated. Who filed the police report?

The RPD found an inconsistency in that the Appellant stated in her BOC that her son attempted unsuccessfully to file police complaints for incidents regarding the looting of his XXXX and life threats. The Appellant testified, however, that it was her son's friend, Mr. XXXX, and that Mr. XXXX tried to file a police complaint. The RPD drew a negative credibility inference concerning this inconsistency. Findings - Inconsistency regarding who filed police report is a material inconsistency

I agree with the RPD that there is an inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence where she stated in her BOC18 that her son filed a police report, but she testified that it was her son-in-law and friend that filed it.19 When the RPD asked about the inconsistency, the Appellant responded that she is getting old and did not remember. I do not find that this explanation is reasonable because it was the information in the BOC that was incorrect while her testimony was correct and supported her son-in-law's affidavit. In submitting her BOC, the Appellant had the benefit of Counsel and time to provide a correction if there were errors. Although this was an inconsistency, I do not find the inconsistency to be sufficiently material to draw a negative inference. While I do not find the RPD's finding to be correct, I re-iterate that I find the RPD's overall credibility assessment to be correct. XXXX 2019 home invasions

The RPD found an inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence between what she stated in her BOC and her testimony concerning incidents at her home in XXXX 2019. The RPD also noted that Mr. XXXX did not mention the home invasion in his affidavit despite being given extensive details about the XXXX XXXX looting.
Although the Appellant states that she filed a police report about this incident and it was reported in the newspaper, none of those documents were submitted at the hearing.

The RPD also stated that it appears that the assailants in the XXXX 2019 home invasion were after her son and not her, as they could have harmed her but did not, although she testified that they said they wanted to kill her also. Findings

I find that the RPD was correct in drawing a negative credibility inference concerning the incidents in XXXX 2019. According to the Appellant's BOC, two men "attacked" her home in search of the Appellant's son. She also stated that, on XXXX XXXX and XXXX, 2019, two men knocked on door of the family's home in search of the Appellant's son and that her son received further threats after this time.20 However, when the RPD asked if anything happened when she was in India in XXXX 2019, she only referred to one incident. The Appellant did not respond to the RPD's question of whether there were other incidents.21

I find that the RPD's finding that the XXXX 2019 incident did not occur to be correct. The testimony given by the Appellant would suggest that there was only one attack, in contrast to the description of the events in her BOC. I do not find it reasonable that the Appellant would not confirm in her testimony that there were two additional attacks and further threats. According to the Appellant, the events in XXXX 2019 were so threatening to her that she was forced to flee the country. However, as she testified, it appears that there was only one event that established this fear while her BOC suggests it was multiple incidents over a period of time. The Appellant was given the opportunity to expand on what happened in XXXX 2019, but she did not do so.

The Appellant also testified that the incident was reported in the newspaper22 and that she filed a police complaint. However, those documents were not filed in evidence. A newspaper article was filed, but the translation of that article does not refer to the XXXX 2019 incident. The Appellant did not respond to the RPD's question as to whether she has a copy of the complaint she filed with the police.23 The RPD also correctly noted that the attack and threats were directly targeting the Appellant's son, as she testified that the assailants yelled "Let XXXX XXXX come out."24 When the RPD then asked the Appellant if the attackers were looking for her son and not her, she said that they would kill her also, if they did not find her son.25 The Appellant only mentioned the threats against her son and his family concerning the XXXX incidents in her BOC. I find that the Appellant embellished her testimony in response to the RPD's questions. As with the RPD, it is important to note that the Appellant's son-in-law, Mr. XXXX, did not mention the XXXX incidents in his affidavit, which is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 although he does discuss the issues with the XXXX XXXX. I find that the evidence supports the proposition that, if the DSS were threatening the Appellant's family, they were targeting the Appellant's son and not her specifically.

I find that the RPD is correct in finding that the incident in XXXX 2019 did not occur, regardless of whether the alleged focus was on the Appellant or her son. I find that, if any events did occur, it did not occur in the way the Appellant describes it. I should also note that there is no evidence as to the identity of the attackers in the XXXX incidents, only that they were men with swords. There is no evidence that they were connected to the DSS. Delay

The RPD noted that the Appellant waited nearly eight months after the XXXX 2019 home invasion. However, the RPD did not make a finding, stating that it was aware that the Appellant had health conditions for some time that may have clouded her judgement.

I find that the RPD's finding that no negative inference should be made in this regard is reasonable. The Appellant submitted medical records that I discuss below which establishes that she did have health concerns during this time period. Summary of Credibility Findings

I find that the RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant has not provided sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to establish her claim. I find that the RPD was correct where it found a number of inconsistencies in the Appellant's evidence pertaining to a stone throwing incident in 2007, why a police complaint was not filed with respect to that incident, circumstances surrounding the looting of the Appellant's son's XXXX XXXX, and the alleged XXXX 2019 attacks at her home. I found the inconsistencies concerning who filed the police complaint after the XXXX XXXX incident and the omission of mentioning that Mr. XXXX is the Appellant's son-in-law not to be material. Although I found these inconsistencies not to be material, it does not affect my overall finding. After a review of the transcript and all of the documentary evidence, I find that the Appellant has not provided sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence that she faces a risk of persecution or a risk of harm.26 There is a lack of credible and trustworthy evidence that the Appellant has ever been targeted by the DSS, that the DSS is either responsible for the rock throwing incident or the attack on her home, or if they were responsible, and that the Appellant was the intended recipient of the threats. If the DSS were responsible for the looting of the Appellant's son's XXXX, they were not targeting the Appellant.

The Appellant has submitted a number of medical records27 to establish that she had health problems and a surgery in XXXX 2021. The RPD acknowledged the Appellant's health challenges in its decision. The Appellant has not provided submissions that the material inconsistencies in her testimony and evidence relate to her health conditions. Although I recognize that the stress of a hearing can affects one's recollection, I find that the Appellant's inconsistencies in the Appellant's testimony and evidence cannot be explained by way of previous health conditions. Other grounds of appeal submitted by the Appellant

As I understand the Appellant's Legal Memorandum, the Appellant raises three grounds of appeal. First, the Immigration and Refugee Board's (IRB's) Guideline 4, Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution (Guideline 4)28 was not mentioned by the RPD. Second, the RPD erred in conducting its analysis of sections 96 and 97 of the Appellant's claim. Third, the Appellant submits that the RPD erred in not reviewing the documentary evidence. The Appellant also states that the RPD failed to analyze the Appellant's personalized risk, and it did not review all of the grounds, even those not raised by the Appellant. Guideline 4 was respected by the RPD

Under the heading of "standard of review," the Appellant makes reference to the fact that the RPD did not refer to Guideline 4. However, the Appellant did not provide any specific submissions with respect to this reference or explain the relevance of the Guideline in this appeal.

Without any submissions, I have no basis to understand in what way the Appellant suggests that the RPD did not follow Guideline 4. I acknowledge that the RPD did not cite Guideline 4. However, I have reviewed the transcript, along with the Appellant's documentary evidence, and I do not find that the RPD erred with respect to the application of Guideline 4 in terms of assessing the Appellant's evidence or the challenges that may occur at the hearing. The RPD did not err in conducting its analysis of sections 96 and 97 of the Appellant's case

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its analysis of sections 96 and 97. The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to analyze whether there is a nexus between the Appellant's claim and a Convention ground based on section 96 or 97 of the IRPA. She further submits, in citing Attakora29 and Armson30 that they support of her position and state the following: 22. It is respectfully submitted that the Refugee Protection Division's finding that there is insufficient credible evidence is not determinative of the question of whether the appellants are convention refugees or persons in need of protection. Whether credible or not, a claimant remains a protected person if they are able to satisfy the subjective and objective component of the test in either section 96 or 97 of the Act. 23. The Court of Appeal held that the Refugee Protection Division must rule not only on credibility issues but also on the well-founded fear alleged by the refugee claimant in order to determine whether the evidence satisfies both the objective and subjective branches of the test.
The Appellant submits that credibility is consideration under section 97, but it is not determinative, and that the RPD erred on relying on credibility in rejecting the Appellant's claim.

The Appellant submits that the Bouaouni31 case states that the lack of credibility for a claimant, pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, is not determinative for the section 97 test. She submits that, in order to qualify as a protected person under section 97, a claimant must demonstrate a risk of torture, a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, on a balance of probabilities. The Appellant submits that the caselaw states that section 97 requires the decision-maker to characterize the nature of the risk and, if so, whether the risk is one of cruel and unusual punishment or treatment.32 Findings - The RPD did not err either in its section 96 or section 97 analysis
I find that the RPD did not err in its analysis under either section 96 or 97 of the IRPA.

I am unable to understand one of the Appellant's submission when she states that the RPD failed to recognize the Appellant's nexus to a section 96 Convention ground because the RPD did undertake an analysis under both sections 96 and 97 of the Convention. At any rate, the Appellant did not provide submissions as to the Appellant's nexus to a section 96 Convention ground.

With respect to the Appellant's other submissions, I agree with the general proposition that a person, while not a credible witness, may still be found to have a successful protection claim if both the objective and subjective branches of the test are satisfied. In both the Attakora and the Armson cases, the Courts found that both branches were satisfied even though there were credibility issues with the claimant. In both cases, the Court found that decision-maker found that people involved in political activity against the government were at risk and that the claimants had been involved in political activity which would likely result in their arrests if the claimants returned to their home country. The Court, in Attakora, expressed this proposition in this way: These two findings together, which occur towards the end of the Board's reasons, satisfy both the objective and the subjective branches of the test for refugee status. Whether or not the applicant was a credible witness, and I have already indicated that the Board's reasons for finding him not credible are based in error, that does not prevent him from being a refugee if his political opinions and activities are likely to lead to his arrest and punishment. In those circumstances, the only conclusion that was open to the Board was to find that the applicant was indeed a Convention refugee.

The Appellant also cites the Bouaouni case that states that a negative credibility determination, which may be determinative under section 96 of the IRPA, may not be determinative under section 97, namely, whether a claimant's removal would subject the person to the dangers and risks stipulated in section 97. The Court stated that there may be instances where a claimant is found not to be credible, but the country conditions are such that the claimant's particular circumstances make the claimant a person in need of protection.

The facts and circumstances of these cases can be clearly distinguished from the Appellant's case in this appeal. The RPD found, and I find to be correct, that the Appellant will not face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk of harm owing to her views of the DSS.

In the Appellant's BOC, the Appellant identified two documents in the National Documentation Package (NDP) and a large number of references to other documents.33 I am assuming that the documents she submitted were intended to support her contention that there is objective evidence of the risks posed by the DSS should she return to India.

With respect to the NDP, the Appellant points to two documents. One document in the NDP indicates that the DSS is a "socio-spiritual" organization that was founded in 1948 that preaches humanitarianism and selfless services to others. While some refer to the organization as a multi-religious sect, others refer to it as a cult. The NDP indicates that the DSS is known for its fight against drugs and alcohol abuse and its campaign to stop the spread of the HIV virus. In the IRB's Response to Information Request (RIR) in the NDP, there are reports of clashes between the DSS and Sikh organizations.34 The Appellant did not explain the relevance of any of the documents and, in particular, the second document35 she identified in the NDP. One document the Appellant references is in a previous version of the NDP and, like the current version of the document,36 I have no guidance as to how the information in this document is relevant to the Appellant's claim. There is no indication in either document in the NDP that the DSS targets individuals that have opposing views or individuals with the Appellant's profile. Neither document provides any objective evidence to suggest that the Appellant would face persecution or would be a person in need of protection should she return to India.

The Appellant also provided a number of references to documents pertaining to the DSS. The articles deal with mass castration of 400 DSS devotees, how the DSS acquired land illegally, bribery with the police, the DSS involvement with the police, violence by the DSS when its leader was criminally convicted, allegations of a mass grave at a DSS compound, among a number of other topics. The Appellant provided no specific submissions as to how these references relate to the Appellant or how they support the Appellant's objective fear of persecution or that she is a person in need of protection should she return to India.

I find that there is no objective evidence to establish that the Appellant would face persecution in India owing to her views of the DDS or that she is a person in need of protection should she return to India. I have already found that there is insufficient credible and trustworthy evidence that the DSS has targeted her in the 2007 incident, the alleged looting of her son's XXXX in 2017, or the alleged attack in her home in 2019. Unlike in cases cited by the Appellant, there is no objective evidence that the Appellant would face persecution or a risk of harm owing to the fact that she has expressed negative views of the DSS. I recognize that the Appellant beliefs that she is at risk, but that belief is not supported by credible evidence.37

The onus remains on the Appellant to demonstrate that she is a person in need of protection. I note that, in Bouaouni, the Court ultimately found that the elements of section 97 were not met in that case, which is relevant to this appeal. The Court stated: [42] In the present case the Board found important omissions, contradictions and implausibilities in the applicant's evidence, which led it to conclude that the applicant's story was not credible. I have already determined that these findings were open to the Board. The Board specifically disbelieved the applicant's allegation of arrest, detention and torture by the police forces and provided detailed reasons for its findings. Further, the Board showed an appreciation of the country conditions in Tunisia and specifically considered, in its reasons, the country documentation before it. There is no evidence to suggest that the Board failed to consider evidence before it or that it misapprehended any aspect of the evidence. Apart from the evidence that the Board found to be not credible, there was no other evidence before the board in the country documentation, or elsewhere, that could have led the Board to conclude that the applicant was a person in need of protection....38

The Courts have noted that there should be a separate analysis for both claims under sections 96 and 97; however, one Court noted a finding that the objective element of section 96 had not been met, which, depending on circumstances, may dispose of the section 97 issue as well.39

I find that the RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant has not established that she is a Convention refugee under section 96 or a person in need of protection under section 97. Other grounds submitted by the Appellant

The Appellant further submits that the RPD erred in that it must examine all of the grounds of a refugee protection claim even when they are not raised by the claimant, including risks faced by the claimant.
The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in not showing the legal reasoning to conclude that the claimant is in need of protection and to evaluate the personalized risk if she returns to India.
The Appellant also referenced that the RPD erred by failing to meaningfully engage with the Appellants' documentary evidence that were provided to corroborate the Appellants' allegations.

I find that the RPD did review all relevant grounds for refugee protection. The RPD found that the Appellant had not established with credible and sufficient evidence that she faces a risk of persecution or a risk of harm under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA. The Appellant did not provide any specific submissions on how the RPD erred in terms of what grounds it should have considered or what risks were not considered. The Appellant's bald statement is not supported by any substantive concerns or indication as to where the RPD's assessment was incorrect.

Similarly, I disagree with the Appellant's submission that the RPD erred in assessing the personalized risk should the Appellant return to India. The RPD found, which I find to be correct, that the Appellant has not established with credible and trustworthy evidence that there is a risk of persecution or a risk of harm should she return to India. Without specific submissions, I am unable to ascertain why the Appellant states that the RPD erred in not assessing the personalized risk.

Further, I disagree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in failing to review the documentary evidence. Even if the RPD did not review every document, I have reviewed documents I have considered relevant in my independent assessment of the Appellant's claim. The Appellant submitted a newspaper article which was not specifically referred to but deals with background information pertaining to the DSS.40 In addition, there are two affidavits which I have dealt with in my assessment. I have already made reference to many citations given in the Appellant's BOC that provide background to the DSS. Finally, there are various medical records. The RPD acknowledged the Appellant's medical condition, and I have addressed this issue in my review.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
